newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU oil product surplus grows, crude fall surprises.
newsitem.headline: EU oil product surplus grows, crude fall surprises.

text.p: Further growth of European oil product stocks in February due to high refinery runs was even more bearish than expected, analysts said in response to figures released on Tuesday.
"We were expecting runs to be flat or down. They weren't and they've simply exaggerated the products' surplus," said Mike Barry of Energy Market Consultants.

Middle distillate stocks rose by 7.13 million barrels, or 0.9 percent, to 302.63 million barrels in February, leaving them 28.74 million barrels, or 10.5 percent, higher than a year ago, Stichting Euroilstock said in its latest inventory report.
Month-on-month, middle distillate stocks rose sharpest in the Netherlands (up 4.12 million barrels) and Germany (up 3.00 million barrels).
High refinery output and very mild weather appear to have been the cause. Last February, a cold snap drove prices to what were then three-year highs, eating into stocks.
"We've had totally the opposite weather this year. We believe it was the mildest (February) in seven years," said Barry.
Fuel oil stocks also rose, up 2.08 million barrels, or 1.5 percent, to 141.38 million barrels, resulting in a year-on-year surplus of 3.75 million barrels, or 2.7 percent.
"Distillates and fuel oil have completely bombed out. Only mogas is still tight," said Geoff Pyne, oil analyst at Swiss bank UBS.

Gasoline stocks, though higher at the end of February, were still 7.21 million barrels, or 4.2 percent, lower than a year ago. However, as analysts pointed out, gasoline is rarely a dominant force in the oversupplied European market.
"I really can't see much good news for the market with product levels like these," said Peter Bogin, associate director of oil consultants Cambridge Energy Research Associates.
One scrap of bullish news was a surprise 14.89 million barrel, or 3.7 percent, fall of crude oil stocks, to 392.30 million barrels.
"A slight dip seemed possible, but it was so far from what was expected," said Bogin.

However, few analysts believed the crude draw could fully counter the bearishness of the the product build. The large monthly fall only left crude stocks 980,000 barrels, or 0.2 percent, below year-ago levels.
"That crude draw is not that bullish given seasonal factors. (Crude) stocks are often drawn down at this time of year. The overall position is more than offset by product builds," said UBS's Pyne.
Crude and oil product stocks together rose by 5.55 million barrels, or 0.5 percent, in February but were still 22.55 million barrels, or 2.2 percent higher than in February 1996.
Crude intake was 460,000 barrels per day (bpd) higher than in January at 11.982 million bpd, leading to a utilisation rate of 95.10 percent in February.
